paras: The mob assault on John Dove took place near Fawbush, in the county around Somerset, Kentucky, around the end of December 1880, when a mob of fifty men dragged Dove from his house almost naked and hanged him by the heels. He was found almost dead, and the dispatches doubted he would recover. The story ran first as crime news and then, weeks later, as a widely reprinted joke about "faithless husbands."

According to a Somerset dispatch of January 2, Dove was "a notorious fellow" who had for some time been talking "in slanderous and delightfully free manner" about the wives of several respected citizens. The Chicago Tribune's dispatch, dated December 31, said he was accused of talking too freely about his neighbors' wives and "otherwise rendering himself objectionable." None of the reports gives his race.

A mob of fifty men, masked according to the Tribune, came to Dove's home near Fawbush. They took him out almost naked and hung him by his heels in the cold. When he was found soon afterward he was almost dead; the Tribune said he "will probably die," while the Gazette's dispatch said his recovery was "by no means certain."

The Gazette's correspondent wrote that the affair had created great excitement and that vigorous measures would be taken to bring the lynchers to justice. No report of arrests, of charges, or of whether Dove lived or died was found in the coverage.

The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the first report on January 2 under the headline "BRUTAL TREATMENT," among other crime dispatches, and a Michigan weekly repeated its text without a dateline on January 6. The Daily Gazette's longer version of January 4, headed "HANGED BY THE HEELS," called Dove notorious and stressed his slanders while still calling his attackers lynchers.

From late January a different paragraph circulated, opening, "Public opinion on the subject of faithless husbands is very strong in Somerset, Ky." It ran as filler in the Delaware State Journal, the Southern Standard, the Fayette County Herald, the Iron County Register, the Pioche Weekly Record, the Maryland Republican, the People's Vindicator and the Grant County Herald between January 20 and February 10. Most printings named the man "Mr. Love," but the Pioche paper named him "Mr. Dove."

The joke paragraph told a different story from the dispatches: Dove's wife led the mob, he fled "without coat, trousers, or boots," was overtaken after a mile and left hanging head downward from a tree. In this telling he was almost frozen when a "humane preacher" cut him down two hours later. The dated Somerset dispatches, which blame slander rather than infidelity and name no leader, are the nearer source.

bases: A mob of fifty men took John Dove from his home and hanged him by the heels, leaving him almost dead, but no report says he died (A1, A2).

A mob of fifty acting without authority punished Dove for alleged slander of neighbors' wives, but he was alive when found and no later report of his death appears, so no one is known to have been killed (A1, A2, A8).

Two differently worded Somerset dispatches of Dec. 31 and Jan. 2 agree that a mob of fifty hanged Dove by the heels and left him nearly dead (A1, A2); a later humorous paragraph gives different circumstances (A4, A8).

accounts.label: Somerset wire dispatches
accounts.gist: A mob of fifty (masked, per the Tribune) took Dove almost naked from his house near Fawbush over his talk about neighbors' wives and hanged him by the heels; he was found almost dead.

accounts.label: Humorous paragraph
accounts.gist: His wife led a mob against him as a faithless husband; he fled half-dressed, was overtaken after a mile, left hanging head down from a tree, and was cut down almost frozen by a preacher two hours later.

framing.detail: The Tribune headed it 'BRUTAL TREATMENT' and called the mob 'lynchers' to be brought to justice, while describing Dove as having rendered himself 'objectionable'.
The Gazette's 'HANGED BY THE HEELS' called Dove 'a notorious fellow' who had slandered respected citizens' wives, yet reported measures to punish the lynchers.
A Michigan weekly ran the Tribune text as an undatelined roundup item.
The widely reprinted filler treated the episode as a joke about 'faithless husbands', with a 'humane preacher' as its closing touch.
